A matrix weight is a measurable function \(W:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^{2\times2}\) whose entries are locally integrable and whose values are Hermitian positive definite almost everywhere. Matrix powers are defined by spectral calculus. Write \(|v|\) for the Euclidean norm on \(\mathbb C^2\) and \(\|A\|_{\mathrm{op}}\) for its induced matrix operator norm.

Define
\[
[W]_{A_p}=\sup_I\frac1{|I|}\int_I
\Big(\frac1{|I|}\int_I
\|W(x)^{1/p}W(y)^{-1/p}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^q\,dy\Big)^{p-1}\,dx,
\]
where the supremum runs over all intervals \(I\subset\mathbb R\) of positive finite length and all integrals use Lebesgue measure. For measurable \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^2\), set
\[
\|f\|_{L^p(W)}=\Big(\int_{\mathbb R}|W(x)^{1/p}f(x)|^p\,dx\Big)^{1/p}.
\]
The Hilbert transform acts componentwise on smooth compactly supported vector-valued functions by
\[
Hf(x)=\frac1\pi\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\int_{|x-y|>\varepsilon}\frac{f(y)}{x-y}\,dy.

import os, sympy as sp, numpy as np
from scipy.linalg import fractional_matrix_power
p=sp.symbols('p', positive=True)
q=p/(p-1)
assert sp.simplify(1/p+1/q+q/p**2-(1+1/(p-1)-1/p))==0
assert sp.simplify((q/(q-1))-p)==0
s=sp.symbols('s', positive=True)
t=q*s/(q*s-1)
assert sp.simplify((p-t) - p*(s-1)/ (q*s-1))==0
rng=np.random.default_rng(412)
count=0
for pp in [1.2,1.5,1.9,2.1,3.,5.,10.]:
 for _ in range(50):
  def SPD():
   Z=rng.normal(size=(2,2))+1j*rng.normal(size=(2,2))
   return Z.conj().T@Z+np.eye(2)
  U,V,A,B=SPD(),SPD(),SPD(),SPD()
  z=rng.normal(size=2)+1j*rng.normal(size=2)
  op=lambda Z: np.linalg.norm(Z,2)
  # Directional Ap kernel inequality and Hermitian-product adjoint norm.
  assert op(U@np.linalg.inv(V))+1e-10 >=np.linalg.norm(U@z)/np.linalg.norm(V@z)
  assert np.isclose(op(A@B),op(B@A))
  assert np.isclose(op(np.linalg.inv(A)@U),op(U@np.linalg.inv(A)))
  assert op(A@np.linalg.inv(U)) <= op(A@B)*op(np.linalg.inv(B)@np.linalg.inv(U))+1e-9
  # Pairing factorization through A; np.vdot conjugates first entry.
  f=rng.normal(size=2)+1j*rng.normal(size=2)
  g=rng.normal(size=2)+1j*rng.normal(size=2)
  assert np.allclose(np.vdot(np.linalg.inv(V)@f,U@g),np.vdot(A@np.linalg.inv(V)@f,np.linalg.inv(A)@U@g))
  count+=5
print('Exact symbolic exponent / conjugacy identities: 3 passed')
print('Randomized positive-definite matrix checks:',count,'passed')
os.makedirs('workspace',exist_ok=True)
# Preserve reproducible checks as an ordinary importable script.
source=open(__file__).read()
if not __file__.endswith('agent1_upper_checks.py'):
 open('workspace/agent1_upper_checks.py','w').write(source)

The stated conclusion is a pair of bounds, not an exact formula:
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\max\left\{1,\frac1{p-1}\right\}
\leq \beta(p)
\leq 1+\frac1{p-1}-\frac1p .}
\]
In particular, these bounds do not determine \(\beta(p)\) for \(p\ne2\).

Here is a proof of both bounds, including the quantifiers and smoothness requirement in the lower bound. Computational checks are supplied at the end; they supplement, rather than replace, the analytic proof.

Throughout, constants denoted by \(C_p\) can change from line to line and depend only on \(p\). Write
\[
U=W^{1/p},\qquad K=[W]_{A_p},\qquad
\langle h\rangle_I=\frac1{|I|}\int_Ih.
\]

## 1. Two preliminary estimates

### 1.1 Quantitative scalar reverse Hölder estimate

If a scalar weight \(u\) belongs to \(A_r\), with characteristic \(L\), then
\[
\left\langle u^{1+\delta}\right\rangle_I
\leq 2\langle u\rangle_I^{1+\delta},
\qquad
\delta=\frac{2^{-r}}{16L}.
\tag{1}
\]

Here is a proof with the needed dependence on \(L\). Hölder's inequality and the \(A_r\) condition imply, for \(E\subset J\),
\[
\frac{u(E)}{u(J)}
\geq \frac1L\left(\frac{|E|}{|J|}\right)^r.
\tag{2}
\]
Starting with \(I\), stop on maximal dyadic subintervals \(P\) satisfying
\(\langle u\rangle_P>2\langle u\rangle_I\), and repeat inside each stopped interval. If \(F_k\) is the union of the intervals in generation \(k\), then
\[
|F_k|\leq 2^{-k}|I|,
\qquad
u(F_k)\leq \rho^k u(I),
\quad
\rho=1-\theta,\quad \theta=\frac{2^{-r}}L.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the stopped children occupy at most half their parent's length; apply (2) to their complement. Maximality also gives
\(\langle u\rangle_P\leq4\langle u\rangle_J\) for a stopped child of \(J\).
Consequently, writing \(a=\langle u\rangle_I\),
\[
u(x)\leq 2\cdot4^k a
\quad\text{a.e. on }F_k\setminus F_{k+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_Iu^{1+\delta}
&\leq (2a)^\delta u(I)
 \left[1+\sum_{k\geq1}
 (4^{k\delta}-4^{(k-1)\delta})\rho^k\right]\\
&=(2a)^\delta u(I)\frac{\theta}{1-4^\delta\rho}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(\delta=\theta/16\),
\[
4^\delta\leq1+\theta/4,\qquad
1-4^\delta\rho\geq3\theta/4.
\]
Since \((4/3)2^{1/16}<2\), this proves (1).

### 1.2 A vector sparse estimate for \(H\)

For compactly supported bounded \(a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^2\) and compactly supported integrable \(b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^2\), there is a family \(\mathcal S\) of intervals, with pairwise disjoint measurable sets \(E_J\subset J\) satisfying
\[
|E_J|\geq |J|/6,
\]
such that
\[
\left|\int_{\mathbb R}\langle Ha,b\rangle\right|
\leq C\sum_{J\in\mathcal S}|J|
 \left\langle\left\langle
 |\langle a(y),b(x)\rangle|
 \right\rangle_{y\in J}\right\rangle_{x\in J}.
\tag{4}
\]

For completeness, the sparse construction follows from the following elementary facts about the scalar Hilbert transform.

* Its Fourier multiplier is \(-i\,\operatorname{sgn}\xi\), so its \(L^2\) norm is at most one.
* It is weak type \((1,1)\). To see this, perform the dyadic Calderón–Zygmund decomposition at height \(\lambda\). The good part has squared \(L^2\) norm at most \(C\lambda\|a\|_1\). For a mean-zero bad part \(b_J\), kernel subtraction gives
  \[
  \int_{(3J)^c}|Hb_J|
  \leq C\|b_J\|_1.
  \]
  These estimates give
  \(|\{|Ha|>\lambda\}|\leq C\|a\|_1/\lambda\).
* The grand maximal operator
  \[
  \mathcal M_Ha(x)=
  \sup_{I\ni x}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\xi\in I}
  |H(a1_{(3I)^c})(\xi)|
  \]
  is also weak type \((1,1)\). Indeed, kernel smoothness, followed by choosing a point in \(I\) avoiding two exceptional sets, gives, for \(0<\eta<1\),
  \[
  \mathcal M_Ha\leq C_\eta\bigl(M_\eta(Ha)+Ma\bigr),
  \quad M_\eta h=(M|h|^\eta)^{1/\eta}.
  \]
  The weak bound for \(H\), together with the weak \(L^{1/\eta}\) bound for \(M\), proves the claim. The latter bound follows by splitting a function into the parts below and above half the threshold and applying the weak \((1,1)\) bound for \(M\).

Here are the remaining details of the vector construction. Regard \(\mathbb C^2\) as \(\mathbb R^4\), and define
\[
\mathcal K_J(a)=
\left\{\langle\varphi a\rangle_J:
 \varphi\text{ real-valued},\ |\varphi|\leq1\right\}.
\]
By the symmetric John ellipsoid theorem, on its span one can normalize this body to lie between the Euclidean unit ball and twice that ball. For the correspondingly normalized function \(h\),
\(\langle |h|\rangle_J\leq C\).

On a dyadic interval \(Q\), apply the weak estimates above, coordinatewise, to \(h1_{3Q}\). Choose the exceptional threshold sufficiently large that the exceptional set in \(Q\) has measure at most \(|Q|/8\). The maximal dyadic intervals \(P\subset Q\) on which the exceptional set has density greater than \(1/4\):

* cover the exceptional set up to a null set;
* have total length at most \(|Q|/2\);
* each contain a nonexceptional point.

Off these intervals, the direct Hilbert-transform bound applies. On each \(P\), its nonexceptional point and the grand maximal bound control
\(H(a1_{3Q\setminus3P})\). Undoing the normalization gives
\[
H(a1_{3Q})1_Q
=b_Q+\sum_P H(a1_{3P})1_P,
\qquad
b_Q(x)\in C\mathcal K_{3Q}(a).
\tag{5}
\]
Iterate. Generation \(k\) occupies at most \(2^{-k}|Q|\), so the recursion terminates at almost every point. Pairing the resulting inclusion with \(b\), use
\[
\sup_{v\in\mathcal K_J(a)}
|\operatorname{Re}\langle v,b(x)\rangle|
\leq \left\langle|\langle a(y),b(x)\rangle|\right\rangle_{y\in J}.
\]
The resulting intervals are \(J=3Q\). The original disjoint sparse sets have size at least \(|Q|/2=|J|/6\), proving (4). An initial \(Q\) can be chosen to contain the support of \(b\) and with \(3Q\) containing the support of \(a\).

## 2. Reducing matrices and directional scalar weights

Finiteness of \(K\) implies \(U^{-1}\in L^q_{\rm loc}\). Indeed, on each interval one can choose an \(x_0\) for which \(U(x_0)\) is invertible and
\[
\int_I\|U(x_0)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^q\,dy<\infty.
\]
Then
\[
\|U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
\leq\|U(x_0)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
     \|U(x_0)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Also \(U\in L^p_{\rm loc}\), because \(\|U\|_{\rm op}^p=\|W\|_{\rm op}\).

For each interval \(I\), apply the John ellipsoid theorem to the norms
\[
a_I(v)=\langle|Uv|^p\rangle_I^{1/p},
\qquad
b_I(v)=\langle|U^{-1}v|^q\rangle_I^{1/q}.
\]
Their complex rotational invariance makes the reducing ellipsoids Hermitian. Thus there are positive definite Hermitian matrices \(A_I,B_I\) such that
\[
|A_Iv|\leq a_I(v)\leq2|A_Iv|,
\qquad
|B_Iv|\leq b_I(v)\leq2|B_Iv|.
\tag{6}
\]

Comparison with the two coordinate columns, using the triangle inequality in \(L^p\) and \(L^q\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left\langle
 \left\langle\|U(x)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^{q}
 \right\rangle_{y\in I}^{p/q}
 \right\rangle_{x\in I}^{1/p}
 \asymp_p \|A_IB_I\|_{\rm op}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
For clarity, first take adjoints inside the operator norm and apply the second comparison in (6), columnwise, to obtain
\[
\left\langle\|U(x)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^q
\right\rangle_y^{1/q}
\asymp_q\|U(x)B_I\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Then apply the first comparison in (6), again columnwise. In particular,
\[
\|A_IB_I\|_{\rm op}\leq C_pK^{1/p}.
\tag{8}
\]

Apply the same reasoning to
\[
V=W^{-q/p},\qquad V^{1/q}=U^{-1}.
\]
Its reducing matrices are \(B_I,A_I\), and
\(\|B_IA_I\|_{\rm op}=\|A_IB_I\|_{\rm op}\). Therefore
\[
[V]_{A_q}\leq C_pK^{q/p}.
\tag{9}
\]

Every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb C^2\) gives a scalar weight
\[
w_v(x)=|U(x)v|^p.
\]
The inequality
\[
\|U(x)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
\geq \frac{|U(x)v|}{|U(y)v|}
\]
shows directly that
\[
[w_v]_{A_p}\leq K.
\tag{10}
\]
Similarly, (9) gives
\[
[\,|U^{-1}v|^q\,]_{A_q}\leq C_pK^{q/p}.
\tag{11}
\]

Choose
\[
r-1=c_pK^{-1},\qquad
s-1=c_pK^{-q/p},
\tag{12}
\]
with \(c_p>0\) sufficiently small. Applying (1) to (10)–(11), and then using (6) on the two coordinate vectors, yields
\[
\left\langle\|UA_I^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^{pr}\right\rangle_I^{1/(pr)}
\leq C_p,
\qquad
\left\langle\|U^{-1}B_I^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^{qs}\right\rangle_I^{1/(qs)}
\leq C_p.
\tag{13}
\]

## 3. The upper bound

Let \(f\) be smooth and compactly supported. Put \(F=Uf\), and let \(G\) be bounded and compactly supported. Apply (4) with
\[
a=f=U^{-1}F,\qquad b=UG.
\]
On an interval \(I\), suppress its subscripts on \(A,B\). Since \(A\) is Hermitian,
\[
\langle U(y)^{-1}F(y),U(x)G(x)\rangle
=
\langle AU(y)^{-1}F(y),A^{-1}U(x)G(x)\rangle.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\|AU(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
\leq \|AB\|_{\rm op}
      \|B^{-1}U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Taking adjoints allows (13) to be used on both factors. Hölder's inequality and (8) consequently give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left\langle\left\langle
 |\langle U(y)^{-1}F(y),U(x)G(x)\rangle|
 \right\rangle_y\right\rangle_x\\
&\qquad\leq
 C_pK^{1/p}
 \langle|F|^a\rangle_I^{1/a}
 \langle|G|^b\rangle_I^{1/b},
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
where
\[
a=(qs)'<p,\qquad b=(pr)'<q.
\]

Write \(M_t h=(M|h|^t)^{1/t}\). By the disjoint sparse sets,
\[
\sum_{I\in\mathcal S}|I|
 \langle|F|^a\rangle_I^{1/a}
 \langle|G|^b\rangle_I^{1/b}
\leq6\int M_aF\,M_bG.
\tag{15}
\]
The scalar maximal-function estimate gives
\[
\|M_aF\|_p\leq C_p(s-1)^{-1/p}\|F\|_p,
\qquad
\|M_bG\|_q\leq C_p(r-1)^{-1/q}\|G\|_q.
\tag{16}
\]
There is no loss in these exponents: for example,
\[
p-a=\frac{p(s-1)}{qs-1},
\qquad
\frac1a-\frac1p=\frac{s-1}{qs},
\]
so the additional factor from the usual maximal bound is bounded uniformly for \(0<s-1\leq1\).

Combining (4), (12), and (14)–(16),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|\int\langle Hf,UG\rangle\right|
&\leq C_p
 K^{1/p}K^{q/p^2}K^{1/q}
 \|F\|_p\|G\|_q\\
&=C_pK^{\,1+1/(p-1)-1/p}
 \|f\|_{L^p(W)}\|G\|_q.
\end{aligned}
\]
Duality, first on compact sets and then by increasing those sets, proves
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\|Hf\|_{L^p(W)}
\leq C_p[W]_{A_p}^{\,1+1/(p-1)-1/p}
\|f\|_{L^p(W)}.}
\tag{17}
\]

\leq(2L)^{(1-\varepsilon)/(p-1)}.

Their required product is at most \(4/\varepsilon\).

Define
\[
\rho(t)=
\begin{cases}e^{-1/t},&t>0,\\0,&t\leq0,\end{cases}
\qquad
\eta(t)=\frac{\rho(t)}{\rho(t)+\rho(1-t)},
\qquad \delta=e^{-4/\varepsilon},
\]
and take
\[
\phi_\varepsilon(x)=
\eta(2x/\delta-1)\eta(2-2x).
\]
This is smooth, supported in \([\delta/2,1]\), lies between zero and one, and equals one on \([\delta,1/2]\). Thus
\[
\|\phi_\varepsilon\|_{L^p(w_\varepsilon)}^p\leq1/\varepsilon.
\]
For \(e^{-2/\varepsilon}\leq t\leq e^{-1/\varepsilon}\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|H\phi_\varepsilon(-t)|
&\geq\frac1\pi\int_\delta^{1/2}\frac{dy}{t+y}\\
&=\frac1\pi\log\frac{t+1/2}{t+\delta}
\geq\frac1{2\pi\varepsilon}.
\end{aligned}
\]
It follows that, for \(f_\varepsilon=\phi_\varepsilon e_1\),
\[
\frac{\|Hf_\varepsilon\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}}
{\|f_\varepsilon\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}}
\geq
\frac{(e^{-1}-e^{-2})^{1/p}}{2\pi\varepsilon}.
\tag{20}
\]
For every \(\gamma<1\), the ratio of (20) to
\([W_\varepsilon]_{A_p}^{\gamma}\) tends to infinity. Hence
\[
\beta(p)\geq1.
\tag{21}
\]

## 5. Lower bound \(1/(p-1)\)

Now put
\[
\alpha=(p-1)(1-\varepsilon),\qquad
w_\varepsilon(x)=|x|^\alpha,\qquad
W_\varepsilon=w_\varepsilon I_2,
\quad 0<\varepsilon<1.
\]
Then
\[
[W_\varepsilon]_{A_p}
\leq(2/\varepsilon)^{p-1}.
\tag{22}
\]
For an interval \((a,b)\) on the positive side, put \(r=a/b\). Its averages satisfy
\[
\langle w_\varepsilon\rangle\leq b^\alpha,
\]
and
\[
\left\langle w_\varepsilon^{-1/(p-1)}\right\rangle
=b^{-1+\varepsilon}
 \frac{1-r^\varepsilon}{\varepsilon(1-r)}
\leq \frac{b^{-1+\varepsilon}}{\varepsilon},
\]
because \(r^\varepsilon\geq r\). Negative intervals are identical. For an interval crossing zero, with \(R\) the larger endpoint magnitude,
\[
\langle w_\varepsilon\rangle\leq R^\alpha,\qquad
\left\langle w_\varepsilon^{-1/(p-1)}\right\rangle
\leq2R^{-1+\varepsilon}/\varepsilon.
\]
This proves (22).

Initially use
\[
f(x)=x^{-1+\varepsilon}1_{(0,1)}(x)e_1.
\]
A direct calculation gives
\[
\|f\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}^p
=\int_0^1x^{-1+\varepsilon}\,dx
=1/\varepsilon.
\]
For \(0<t<1\),
\[
|Hf(-t)|
\geq\frac1\pi\int_0^t\frac{y^{-1+\varepsilon}}{2t}\,dy
=\frac{t^{-1+\varepsilon}}{2\pi\varepsilon}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\|Hf\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}^p
\geq(2\pi\varepsilon)^{-p}/\varepsilon.
\tag{23}
\]

To obtain admissible smooth inputs, use the same function \(\eta\) as above and set, on \(0<x<1\),
\[
f_n(x)=x^{-1+\varepsilon}\eta(nx)\eta(n(1-x))e_1,
\]
and zero elsewhere. These are smooth compactly supported functions: the exponential cutoffs vanish to infinite order at both endpoints. They satisfy \(|f_n|\leq|f|\) and converge pointwise to \(f\).

Dominated convergence gives convergence of their input norms. On the negative half-line, the Hilbert integrals converge pointwise by dominated convergence; Fatou's lemma and (23) therefore give
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\frac{\|Hf_n\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}}
{\|f_n\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}}
\geq\frac1{2\pi\varepsilon}.
\]
In particular, some \(n\) has ratio greater than \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon)\).

Given any \(\gamma<1/(p-1)\) and any finite \(C>0\), choose \(\varepsilon\) so small that
\[
\frac1{4\pi\varepsilon}
>C(2/\varepsilon)^{(p-1)\gamma}.
\]
Then this \(W_\varepsilon\) and the corresponding smooth \(f_n\) satisfy the strict inequality requested in the question. Thus
\[
\beta(p)\geq\frac1{p-1}.
\tag{24}
\]

Together, (17), (21), and (24) prove the asserted bounds.

Here is a proof of both bounds, including the quantifiers and smoothness requirement in the lower bound. Computational checks are supplied at the end; they supplement, rather than replace, the analytic proof.

Throughout, constants denoted by \(C_p\) can change from line to line and depend only on \(p\). Write
\[
U=W^{1/p},\qquad K=[W]_{A_p},\qquad
\langle h\rangle_I=\frac1{|I|}\int_Ih.
\]

## 1. Two preliminary estimates

### 1.1 Quantitative scalar reverse Hölder estimate

If a scalar weight \(u\) belongs to \(A_r\), with characteristic \(L\), then
\[
\left\langle u^{1+\delta}\right\rangle_I
\leq 2\langle u\rangle_I^{1+\delta},
\qquad
\delta=\frac{2^{-r}}{16L}.
\tag{1}
\]

Here is a proof with the needed dependence on \(L\). Hölder's inequality and the \(A_r\) condition imply, for \(E\subset J\),
\[
\frac{u(E)}{u(J)}
\geq \frac1L\left(\frac{|E|}{|J|}\right)^r.
\tag{2}
\]
Starting with \(I\), stop on maximal dyadic subintervals \(P\) satisfying
\(\langle u\rangle_P>2\langle u\rangle_I\), and repeat inside each stopped interval. If \(F_k\) is the union of the intervals in generation \(k\), then
\[
|F_k|\leq 2^{-k}|I|,
\qquad
u(F_k)\leq \rho^k u(I),
\quad
\rho=1-\theta,\quad \theta=\frac{2^{-r}}L.
\tag{3}
\]
Indeed, the stopped children occupy at most half their parent's length; apply (2) to their complement. Maximality also gives
\(\langle u\rangle_P\leq4\langle u\rangle_J\) for a stopped child of \(J\).
Consequently, writing \(a=\langle u\rangle_I\),
\[
u(x)\leq 2\cdot4^k a
\quad\text{a.e. on }F_k\setminus F_{k+1}.
\]
Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\int_Iu^{1+\delta}
&\leq (2a)^\delta u(I)
 \left[1+\sum_{k\geq1}
 (4^{k\delta}-4^{(k-1)\delta})\rho^k\right]\\
&=(2a)^\delta u(I)\frac{\theta}{1-4^\delta\rho}.
\end{aligned}
\]
For \(\delta=\theta/16\),
\[
4^\delta\leq1+\theta/4,\qquad
1-4^\delta\rho\geq3\theta/4.
\]
Since \((4/3)2^{1/16}<2\), this proves (1).

### 1.2 A vector sparse estimate for \(H\)

For compactly supported bounded \(a:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^2\) and compactly supported integrable \(b:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C^2\), there is a family \(\mathcal S\) of intervals, with pairwise disjoint measurable sets \(E_J\subset J\) satisfying
\[
|E_J|\geq |J|/6,
\]
such that
\[
\left|\int_{\mathbb R}\langle Ha,b\rangle\right|
\leq C\sum_{J\in\mathcal S}|J|
 \left\langle\left\langle
 |\langle a(y),b(x)\rangle|
 \right\rangle_{y\in J}\right\rangle_{x\in J}.
\tag{4}
\]

For completeness, the sparse construction follows from the following elementary facts about the scalar Hilbert transform.

* Its Fourier multiplier is \(-i\,\operatorname{sgn}\xi\), so its \(L^2\) norm is at most one.
* It is weak type \((1,1)\). To see this, perform the dyadic Calderón–Zygmund decomposition at height \(\lambda\). The good part has squared \(L^2\) norm at most \(C\lambda\|a\|_1\). For a mean-zero bad part \(b_J\), kernel subtraction gives
  \[
  \int_{(3J)^c}|Hb_J|
  \leq C\|b_J\|_1.
  \]
  These estimates give
  \(|\{|Ha|>\lambda\}|\leq C\|a\|_1/\lambda\).
* The grand maximal operator
  \[
  \mathcal M_Ha(x)=
  \sup_{I\ni x}\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{\xi\in I}
  |H(a1_{(3I)^c})(\xi)|
  \]
  is also weak type \((1,1)\). Indeed, kernel smoothness, followed by choosing a point in \(I\) avoiding two exceptional sets, gives, for \(0<\eta<1\),
  \[
  \mathcal M_Ha\leq C_\eta\bigl(M_\eta(Ha)+Ma\bigr),
  \quad M_\eta h=(M|h|^\eta)^{1/\eta}.
  \]
  The weak bound for \(H\), together with the weak \(L^{1/\eta}\) bound for \(M\), proves the claim. The latter bound follows by splitting a function into the parts below and above half the threshold and applying the weak \((1,1)\) bound for \(M\).

Here are the remaining details of the vector construction. Regard \(\mathbb C^2\) as \(\mathbb R^4\), and define
\[
\mathcal K_J(a)=
\left\{\langle\varphi a\rangle_J:
 \varphi\text{ real-valued},\ |\varphi|\leq1\right\}.
\]
By the symmetric John ellipsoid theorem, on its span one can normalize this body to lie between the Euclidean unit ball and twice that ball. For the correspondingly normalized function \(h\),
\(\langle |h|\rangle_J\leq C\).

On a dyadic interval \(Q\), apply the weak estimates above, coordinatewise, to \(h1_{3Q}\). Choose the exceptional threshold sufficiently large that the exceptional set in \(Q\) has measure at most \(|Q|/8\). The maximal dyadic intervals \(P\subset Q\) on which the exceptional set has density greater than \(1/4\):

* cover the exceptional set up to a null set;
* have total length at most \(|Q|/2\);
* each contain a nonexceptional point.

Off these intervals, the direct Hilbert-transform bound applies. On each \(P\), its nonexceptional point and the grand maximal bound control
\(H(a1_{3Q\setminus3P})\). Undoing the normalization gives
\[
H(a1_{3Q})1_Q
=b_Q+\sum_P H(a1_{3P})1_P,
\qquad
b_Q(x)\in C\mathcal K_{3Q}(a).
\tag{5}
\]
Iterate. Generation \(k\) occupies at most \(2^{-k}|Q|\), so the recursion terminates at almost every point. Pairing the resulting inclusion with \(b\), use
\[
\sup_{v\in\mathcal K_J(a)}
|\operatorname{Re}\langle v,b(x)\rangle|
\leq \left\langle|\langle a(y),b(x)\rangle|\right\rangle_{y\in J}.
\]
The resulting intervals are \(J=3Q\). The original disjoint sparse sets have size at least \(|Q|/2=|J|/6\), proving (4). An initial \(Q\) can be chosen to contain the support of \(b\) and with \(3Q\) containing the support of \(a\).

## 2. Reducing matrices and directional scalar weights

Finiteness of \(K\) implies \(U^{-1}\in L^q_{\rm loc}\). Indeed, on each interval one can choose an \(x_0\) for which \(U(x_0)\) is invertible and
\[
\int_I\|U(x_0)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^q\,dy<\infty.
\]
Then
\[
\|U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
\leq\|U(x_0)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
     \|U(x_0)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Also \(U\in L^p_{\rm loc}\), because \(\|U\|_{\rm op}^p=\|W\|_{\rm op}\).

For each interval \(I\), apply the John ellipsoid theorem to the norms
\[
a_I(v)=\langle|Uv|^p\rangle_I^{1/p},
\qquad
b_I(v)=\langle|U^{-1}v|^q\rangle_I^{1/q}.
\]
Their complex rotational invariance makes the reducing ellipsoids Hermitian. Thus there are positive definite Hermitian matrices \(A_I,B_I\) such that
\[
|A_Iv|\leq a_I(v)\leq2|A_Iv|,
\qquad
|B_Iv|\leq b_I(v)\leq2|B_Iv|.
\tag{6}
\]

Comparison with the two coordinate columns, using the triangle inequality in \(L^p\) and \(L^q\), gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left\langle
 \left\langle\|U(x)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^{q}
 \right\rangle_{y\in I}^{p/q}
 \right\rangle_{x\in I}^{1/p}
 \asymp_p \|A_IB_I\|_{\rm op}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{7}
\]
For clarity, first take adjoints inside the operator norm and apply the second comparison in (6), columnwise, to obtain
\[
\left\langle\|U(x)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^q
\right\rangle_y^{1/q}
\asymp_q\|U(x)B_I\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Then apply the first comparison in (6), again columnwise. In particular,
\[
\|A_IB_I\|_{\rm op}\leq C_pK^{1/p}.
\tag{8}
\]

Apply the same reasoning to
\[
V=W^{-q/p},\qquad V^{1/q}=U^{-1}.
\]
Its reducing matrices are \(B_I,A_I\), and
\(\|B_IA_I\|_{\rm op}=\|A_IB_I\|_{\rm op}\). Therefore
\[
[V]_{A_q}\leq C_pK^{q/p}.
\tag{9}
\]

Every nonzero \(v\in\mathbb C^2\) gives a scalar weight
\[
w_v(x)=|U(x)v|^p.
\]
The inequality
\[
\|U(x)U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
\geq \frac{|U(x)v|}{|U(y)v|}
\]
shows directly that
\[
[w_v]_{A_p}\leq K.
\tag{10}
\]
Similarly, (9) gives
\[
[\,|U^{-1}v|^q\,]_{A_q}\leq C_pK^{q/p}.
\tag{11}
\]

Choose
\[
r-1=c_pK^{-1},\qquad
s-1=c_pK^{-q/p},
\tag{12}
\]
with \(c_p>0\) sufficiently small. Applying (1) to (10)–(11), and then using (6) on the two coordinate vectors, yields
\[
\left\langle\|UA_I^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^{pr}\right\rangle_I^{1/(pr)}
\leq C_p,
\qquad
\left\langle\|U^{-1}B_I^{-1}\|_{\rm op}^{qs}\right\rangle_I^{1/(qs)}
\leq C_p.
\tag{13}
\]

## 3. The upper bound

Let \(f\) be smooth and compactly supported. Put \(F=Uf\), and let \(G\) be bounded and compactly supported. Apply (4) with
\[
a=f=U^{-1}F,\qquad b=UG.
\]
On an interval \(I\), suppress its subscripts on \(A,B\). Since \(A\) is Hermitian,
\[
\langle U(y)^{-1}F(y),U(x)G(x)\rangle
=
\langle AU(y)^{-1}F(y),A^{-1}U(x)G(x)\rangle.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\|AU(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}
\leq \|AB\|_{\rm op}
      \|B^{-1}U(y)^{-1}\|_{\rm op}.
\]
Taking adjoints allows (13) to be used on both factors. Hölder's inequality and (8) consequently give
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left\langle\left\langle
 |\langle U(y)^{-1}F(y),U(x)G(x)\rangle|
 \right\rangle_y\right\rangle_x\\
&\qquad\leq
 C_pK^{1/p}
 \langle|F|^a\rangle_I^{1/a}
 \langle|G|^b\rangle_I^{1/b},
\end{aligned}
\tag{14}
\]
where
\[
a=(qs)'<p,\qquad b=(pr)'<q.
\]

Write \(M_t h=(M|h|^t)^{1/t}\). By the disjoint sparse sets,
\[
\sum_{I\in\mathcal S}|I|
 \langle|F|^a\rangle_I^{1/a}
 \langle|G|^b\rangle_I^{1/b}
\leq6\int M_aF\,M_bG.
\tag{15}
\]
The scalar maximal-function estimate gives
\[
\|M_aF\|_p\leq C_p(s-1)^{-1/p}\|F\|_p,
\qquad
\|M_bG\|_q\leq C_p(r-1)^{-1/q}\|G\|_q.
\tag{16}
\]
There is no loss in these exponents: for example,
\[
p-a=\frac{p(s-1)}{qs-1},
\qquad
\frac1a-\frac1p=\frac{s-1}{qs},
\]
so the additional factor from the usual maximal bound is bounded uniformly for \(0<s-1\leq1\).

Combining (4), (12), and (14)–(16),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\left|\int\langle Hf,UG\rangle\right|
&\leq C_p
 K^{1/p}K^{q/p^2}K^{1/q}
 \|F\|_p\|G\|_q\\
&=C_pK^{\,1+1/(p-1)-1/p}
 \|f\|_{L^p(W)}\|G\|_q.
\end{aligned}
\]
Duality, first on compact sets and then by increasing those sets, proves
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle
\|Hf\|_{L^p(W)}
\leq C_p[W]_{A_p}^{\,1+1/(p-1)-1/p}
\|f\|_{L^p(W)}.}
\tag{17}
\]

Dominated convergence gives convergence of their input norms. On the negative half-line, the Hilbert integrals converge pointwise by dominated convergence; Fatou's lemma and (23) therefore give
\[
\liminf_{n\to\infty}
\frac{\|Hf_n\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}}
{\|f_n\|_{L^p(W_\varepsilon)}}
\geq\frac1{2\pi\varepsilon}.
\]
In particular, some \(n\) has ratio greater than \(1/(4\pi\varepsilon)\).

Given any \(\gamma<1/(p-1)\) and any finite \(C>0\), choose \(\varepsilon\) so small that
\[
\frac1{4\pi\varepsilon}
>C(2/\varepsilon)^{(p-1)\gamma}.
\]
Then this \(W_\varepsilon\) and the corresponding smooth \(f_n\) satisfy the strict inequality requested in the question. Thus
\[
\beta(p)\geq\frac1{p-1}.
\tag{24}
\]

Together, (17), (21), and (24) prove the asserted bounds.
